new_statements.quote: The pitch contours are ordinarily distributed over entire words; that is, they distribute over a root and any affixes it may take. In general, affixes have no independent tone, but a few, recently developed from verbal or nominal roots, do possess independent tones. In compounds, however, each element has its own tone. 2.4 Stress. Words are stressed on the first syllable of the root; this is true also of compounds, which are stressed on the first element of the compound.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Nar-Phu (Nar dialect) is a four-tone word-tone language (tones 1-4, two murmured, two falling; contour spreads over root + affixes). Independently of tone, word stress falls on the first syllable of the root; since the language is 'overwhelmingly suffixing' with a single prefix (negative a-, p. 340), this is word-initial stress in all but negated verb forms. Compounds are stressed on their first element.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Implicitly the negative prefix a- (the only prefix) would precede the stressed root-initial syllable; compounds keep a separate tone on each element but stress only on the first element.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the word = root plus suffixes (the same domain over which the word-tone contour spreads); statement is impressionistic (no acoustic evidence), from the author's own NSF-funded fieldwork on the Nar village dialect. Stress co-exists with a 4-way lexical word-tone contrast, so a cataloguer may prefer to code this as 'tonal-with-stress-statement' with position = root-initial.
new_statements.identity_note: Noonan 2003 states explicitly (p. 336): 'This chapter describes the Nar dialect only' (village of Nar; Mazaudon's 'Nar-mä / lower Nar', vs. Phu = 'Nar-tö / upper Nar'). Glottolog treats Nar and Phu as dialects of narp1239; the statement is for the Nar dialect.
